---
title: "Translating a notice from English to French"
subtitle: "Generate English-to-French translations. Examine the preserved details."
description: "Learn how a local machine-translation checkpoint changes language while preserving the source message."
categories: [natural language generation, machine translation, evaluation]
---

An archive sends short notices to English- and French-speaking visitors. A
translation must change the language while preserving the people, quantities,
dates, permissions, and limits in the source.

The model in this lesson has one direction: English to French. The checkpoint,
or saved model, fixes that direction. The model does not choose a language from
each input. Adding a target-language label to the output does not change the
translation direction.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- load a fixed revision of the English-to-French model and tokenizer locally
- keep constructed source records and generated translations linked to IDs
- count source tokens against the checkpoint's 512-token input limit
- compare translation with a source-copy baseline
- examine names, numbers, and negation without treating these checks as adequacy scores
- reserve meaning and register judgments for a bilingual reviewer.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load one local translation direction

`huggingfaceR::hf_load_tokenizer()` and
`huggingfaceR::hf_load_pipeline()` load the prepared local snapshot through the
course helper. Offline mode prevents a render-time download. The model and
tokenizer files came from the same immutable revision.

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(huggingfaceR)
  library(jsonlite)
  library(purrr)
  library(reticulate)
  library(stringr)
  library(tibble)
  library(tidyr)
})

source("R/use-nlg.R")

translation_model <- load_nlg_pipeline(
  "opus_en_fr",
  "translation"
)

model_record <- translation_model$metadata |>
  select(model_id, revision, license, task_scope)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  model_record,
  col.names = c("Model", "Revision", "License", "Course task"),
  caption = "Pinned local checkpoint for English-to-French translation",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  all(c(
    "dplyr", "huggingfaceR", "jsonlite", "purrr",
    "reticulate", "stringr", "tibble", "tidyr"
  ) %in% loadedNamespaces()),
  identical(
    model_record$model_id,
    "Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-fr"
  ),
  identical(
    model_record$revision,
    "dd7f6540a7a48a7f4db59e5c0b9c42c8eea67f18"
  ),
  identical(model_record$license, "Apache-2.0")
)
```

The package also exports `hf_translate()`, which calls a remote inference
service. This lesson does not use that service. Generation uses the local model
object from the fixed pipeline.

## Read direction from the checkpoint

The local tokenizer configuration names English as the source and French as
the target. A different direction requires a different checkpoint.

```{r}
tokenizer_config_path <- file.path(
  "data-raw",
  ".cache",
  "nlg-models",
  translation_model$metadata$local_directory,
  "tokenizer_config.json"
)
generation_config_path <- file.path(
  "data-raw",
  ".cache",
  "nlg-models",
  translation_model$metadata$local_directory,
  "generation_config.json"
)

tokenizer_config <- fromJSON(tokenizer_config_path)
generation_config <- fromJSON(generation_config_path)

direction <- tibble(
  checkpoint = translation_model$metadata$model_id,
  source_language = tokenizer_config$source_lang,
  target_language = tokenizer_config$target_lang,
  runtime_language_switch = FALSE,
  checkpoint_beams = generation_config$num_beams
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  direction,
  col.names = c(
    "Checkpoint",
    "Source",
    "Target",
    "Runtime direction switch",
    "Checkpoint beams"
  ),
  caption = "Translation direction recorded in the tokenizer configuration",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  file.exists(tokenizer_config_path),
  file.exists(generation_config_path),
  identical(direction$source_language, "en"),
  identical(direction$target_language, "fr"),
  identical(direction$runtime_language_switch, FALSE),
  identical(direction$checkpoint_beams, 4L)
)
```

## Prepare constructed notices

The author wrote these four English notices for the lesson. They are demonstrations,
not human reference translations, a held-out test set, or a population quality
benchmark.

```{r}
translation_inputs <- tribble(
  ~source_id, ~source_text, ~protected_name, ~requires_negation,
  "MT-01",
  "Maya Chen will open Room 5 on 14 September.",
  "Maya Chen",
  FALSE,
  "MT-02",
  "The library did not cancel the workshop.",
  "",
  TRUE,
  "MT-03",
  "Visitors must bring 2 forms.",
  "",
  FALSE,
  "MT-04",
  "The volunteers may use 12 computers on Tuesday.",
  "",
  FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  translation_inputs,
  col.names = c(
    "Source ID",
    "Constructed English source",
    "Protected name",
    "Negation required"
  ),
  caption = "Constructed records for the translation demonstration",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(translation_inputs$source_id, paste0("MT-0", 1:4)),
  !anyDuplicated(translation_inputs$source_id),
  identical(sum(translation_inputs$requires_negation), 1L)
)
```

## Count tokens before calling the model

Marian tokenizes words into subword units, which can represent parts of words.
Its configured input limit is 512 tokens. This lesson disables truncation
because removing the end of a notice can remove essential meaning.

```{r}
translation_budget <- translation_inputs |>
  mutate(
    input_tokens = map_int(
      source_text,
      \(text) nlg_token_count(translation_model$tokenizer, text)
    ),
    model_input_limit = 512L,
    fits_without_truncation = input_tokens <= model_input_limit
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  translation_budget |>
    select(source_id, input_tokens, model_input_limit, fits_without_truncation),
  col.names = c(
    "Source ID",
    "Tokenizer units",
    "Input limit",
    "Fits without truncation"
  ),
  caption = "The workflow compares input counts with the limit before translation",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  all(translation_budget$input_tokens > 0L),
  all(translation_budget$fits_without_truncation),
  all(translation_budget$model_input_limit == 512L)
)
```

For a longer source, setting `truncation = TRUE` would discard source tokens.
This setting would cause data loss. A production workflow would divide the
document into sections or stop for human checks.

## Generate French candidates

The source text goes directly to the encoder. The checkpoint uses four-beam
generation by default, which compares four candidate sequences. The course
helper instead uses `num_beams = 1` and `do_sample = FALSE`. This deterministic
greedy choice selects the highest-scoring next token and keeps the teaching
workflow consistent. It does not imply that the four-beam setting is
nondeterministic or inferior.

The output limit is 80 newly generated tokens. The returned record shows
whether the decoder emitted its end-of-sequence token, or EOS. A separate field
records whether generation used the full output allowance. Both fields can be
`TRUE` when the checkpoint forces EOS at the limit. Neither field proves that the
translation is complete for a reader.

```{r}
translation_results <- translation_budget |>
  mutate(
    generation = map(
      source_text,
      \(text) {
        nlg_generate(
          translation_model,
          text,
          max_new_tokens = 80L
        )
      }
    ),
    french_candidate = map_chr(generation, "text"),
    output_tokens = map_int(generation, "output_tokens"),
    ended_by_eos = map_lgl(generation, "ended_by_eos"),
    hit_token_cap = map_lgl(generation, "hit_token_cap"),
    source_copy_baseline = source_text
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  translation_results |>
    select(source_id, source_text, french_candidate, source_copy_baseline),
  col.names = c(
    "Source ID",
    "English source",
    "Generated French candidate",
    "Untranslated copy baseline"
  ),
  caption = "Real local translations beside a no-translation baseline",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  all(nzchar(translation_results$french_candidate)),
  all(translation_results$output_tokens > 0L),
  all(translation_results$output_tokens <= 80L),
  all(
    translation_results$ended_by_eos |
      translation_results$hit_token_cap
  ),
  any(
    translation_results$french_candidate !=
      translation_results$source_copy_baseline
  )
)
```

The copy baseline preserves the English source exactly and performs no
translation. A changed string alone does not establish a successful translation.

## Examine visible details

The next checks compare exact Arabic numerals and search for the protected
person name. They also search for common French negation markers when the
English source contains `did not`. These checks can find some clear
failures. They cannot establish correct grammar or preservation of the meanings
of `must` and `may`. Nor can they establish an appropriate register, or level of
formality, for the audience.

```{r}
extract_numbers <- function(text) {
  str_extract_all(text, "\\b\\d+\\b")[[1]] |>
    sort()
}

translation_checks <- translation_results |>
  mutate(
    numerals_preserved = map2_lgl(
      source_text,
      french_candidate,
      \(source, output) {
        identical(
          extract_numbers(source),
          extract_numbers(output)
        )
      }
    ),
    name_present = map2_lgl(
      protected_name,
      french_candidate,
      \(name, output) {
        if (!nzchar(name)) {
          NA
        } else {
          str_detect(output, fixed(name))
        }
      }
    ),
    negation_visible = map2_lgl(
      requires_negation,
      french_candidate,
      \(required, output) {
        if (!required) {
          NA
        } else {
          str_detect(
            output,
            regex("\\b(pas|jamais|aucun)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
          )
        }
      }
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    source_id,
    numerals_preserved,
    name_present,
    negation_visible
  )

translation_check_display <- translation_checks |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(numerals_preserved, name_present, negation_visible),
      nlg_screen_label
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  translation_check_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Source ID",
    "Arabic-numeral screen",
    "Protected-name screen",
    "French-negation screen"
  ),
  caption = "Conservative automatic surface checks for the constructed notices",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(translation_checks$source_id, translation_inputs$source_id),
  all(vapply(translation_checks[-1], is.logical, logical(1))),
  identical(nrow(translation_checks), 4L),
  all(is.na(
    translation_checks$name_present[
      !nzchar(translation_inputs$protected_name)
    ]
  )),
  all(is.na(
    translation_checks$negation_visible[
      !translation_inputs$requires_negation
    ]
  ))
)
```

The lesson reports no BLEU or chrF number. These translation-overlap metrics require a documented
reference corpus, preprocessing signature, and corpus-level interpretation.
Even then, one reference cannot represent every acceptable French rendering,
and automatic overlap does not replace bilingual judgment.

`Not flagged by screen` means only that this finite string check found no
problem. It does not establish translation adequacy. `Not applicable` means the
source contained no protected name or negation condition to examine.

## Leave approval to a bilingual reader

```{r}
translation_screen_counts <- translation_checks |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    applicable_screens = sum(!is.na(c_across(c(
      numerals_preserved,
      name_present,
      negation_visible
    )))),
    flagged_screens = sum(c_across(c(
      numerals_preserved,
      name_present,
      negation_visible
    )) %in% FALSE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

translation_review <- tibble(
  review = c(
    "local model execution",
    "source within the 512-token input limit",
    "decoder stopped at EOS or the output cap",
    "surface preservation checks",
    "bilingual meaning and register checks"
  ),
  status = c(
    sprintf(
      "completed: %d candidates",
      sum(nzchar(translation_results$french_candidate))
    ),
    sprintf(
      "within budget: %d/%d candidates",
      sum(translation_budget$fits_without_truncation),
      nrow(translation_budget)
    ),
    sprintf(
      "recorded: %d/%d candidates",
      sum(
        translation_results$ended_by_eos |
          translation_results$hit_token_cap
      ),
      nrow(translation_results)
    ),
    sprintf(
      "scan completed: %d flags across %d applicable checks",
      sum(translation_screen_counts$flagged_screens),
      sum(translation_screen_counts$applicable_screens)
    ),
    "pending"
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  translation_review,
  col.names = c("Check stage", "Status"),
  caption = "Automatic checks do not grant bilingual approval",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  !any(translation_review$status == "passed"),
  identical(tail(translation_review$status, 1L), "pending"),
  all(translation_screen_counts$flagged_screens >= 0L)
)
```

The lesson contains no human ratings. A bilingual reviewer still has to compare
each pair for meaning, tone, register, and natural French.

## What to remember

- Translation changes language while trying to preserve the source message.
- This checkpoint's English-to-French direction is fixed in its model files.
- Count model tokens before generation.
- Treat truncation as data loss.
- Keep an untranslated copy baseline beside generated candidates.
- Names, numbers, and negation checks can reveal errors but cannot prove
  adequacy.
- Human bilingual checks remain necessary before publication.
